t:
(a) 
The Commission shall be supervised by a Board composed of nine members, one of whom shall be the Secretary of Defense or an officer of the Department of Defense designated by the Secretary. Not less than five members of the Board shall be nationals of the United States and the remaining members shall be nationals of the Republic of Panama. At least one of the members of the Board who are nationals of the United States shall be experienced and knowledgeable in the management or operation of an American-flag steamship line which has or had ships regularly transiting the Panama Canal, at least one other such member shall be experienced and knowledgeable in United States port operations or in the business of exporting or importing one of the regular commodities dependent on the Panama Canal as a transportation route, and at least one other such member shall be experienced and knowledgeable in labor matters in the United States. Three members of the Board shall hold no other office in or be employed by the Government of the United States. Members of the Board who are nationals of the United States shall cast their votes as directed by the Secretary of Defense or his designee.
 
    (b) 
The President shall appoint the members of the Board. The members of the Board who are United States nationals shall be appointed by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. Each member of the Board shall hold office at the pleasure of the President and, before assuming the duties of such office, shall take an oath to discharge faithfully the duties of his office. Members of the Board shall serve without compensation but shall be allowed travel or transportation expenses, including per diem in lieu of subsistence, in accordance with section 1107 of this Act.
 
    (c) 
The Board shall hold meetings as provided in regulations adopted by the Commission and approved by the Secretary of Defense. A quorum for the transaction of business shall consist of a majority of the Board members of which a majority of those present are nationals of the United States.

fable.w: The Board supervising the Panama Canal Commission must include people from outside the federal government: Panamanian nationals, members with shipping, port or trade, and labor experience, and three members who hold no other federal office or employment. They serve without compensation, receiving only travel expenses and per diem. The tempting reading is that this merely sets up the governing body of a federal agency whose members are federal officials (like the NLRB), and that U.S. members vote as the Secretary of Defense directs. That reading fails because the required non-federal and foreign members bring outside parties into the federal decision-making.
fable.s: Three members of the Board shall hold no other office in or be employed by the Government of the United States.

opus.w: The Board that supervises the Commission must include members who are not federal employees: some must have shipping, port, trade or labor experience, and others are Panamanian nationals. They serve without pay and receive only travel and per diem, so outside parties take part in federal oversight decisions. The tempting 'No' reading treats this like the NLRB board of paid federal employees in Example 7. That reading fails because the statute requires some members to hold no federal office and to represent outside interests, even though the U.S. members' votes are directed by the Secretary of Defense.
opus.s: Three members of the Board shall hold no other office in or be employed by the Government of the United States.
opus.b: 1. **The tempting reading, and why it fails.** It is tempting to answer "No" by treating this Board like the NLRB in Example 7: an agency's own governing body, appointed by the President with Senate approval, whose U.S. members must "cast their votes as directed by the Secretary of Defense." That reading doesn't hold up. Unlike the paid NLRB members, these members serve without pay and receive only travel and per diem, like the commission in Example 8. Three of them must hold no other federal job, and some must come from industry and labor. The rest are nationals of Panama. So people outside the federal government sit on a body that supervises a federal entity, as with the representative commission in Example 4. Two points make this uncertain: the U.S. members' votes are controlled, and outsiders sitting on an agency's governing board is not a classic advisory role.

qwen_chat.w: The section establishes a Board where US members are required to vote as directed by the Secretary of Defense, making the Board an instrument of the Secretary rather than an independent advisory body of outside experts or public representatives. While Panamanian nationals are members, the definition of participation focuses on consultation with domestic non-federal entities (states, tribes, public, etc.) or granting rights to sue. The US side's involvement is strictly intra-governmental coordination, as the Secretary controls the US votes. Therefore, this does not constitute participation by outside parties in the decision-making process as defined.
qwen_chat.s: Members of the Board who are nationals of the United States shall cast their votes as directed by the Secretary of Defense or his designee.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue "Yes" because the Board includes members who are "nationals of the Republic of Panama" and some US members who "hold no other office in or be employed by the Government of the United States," suggesting outside participation. However, the definition states that Congress, federal agencies, and federal officials are INSIDE the government. The key issue is whether these board members are acting as independent outsiders or as agents of the federal government. The text explicitly states that US members "shall cast their votes as directed by the Secretary of Defense or his designee." This makes the Board an extension of the Secretary of Defense's authority, not an independent advisory body of outsiders. Furthermore, the Board supervises the Commission, which is likely a federal entity. The interaction is primarily internal to the executive branch (Secretary directing votes). Even if Panamanian nationals are involved, the prompt's definition emphasizes that "consultation or coordination BETWEEN federal agencies or federal officials... is not participation." Here, the US members are effectively federal officials acting under direct command. The Panamanian members are part of a bilateral commission structure, but the decision-making power for the US side is centralized in the Secretary. More importantly, the definition says "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision." The Board *is* the decision-making body for the Commission. If the Commission is a federal agency, the Board is its governing body. The US members are federal officials. The Panamanian members are foreign nationals. Does the US government consult with Panamanian nationals? Yes, they are on the board. But is this "participation" as defined? The definition includes "advisory committee, board, or panel that includes non-federal members". Panamanian nationals are non-federal. However, the US members are directed by the Secretary. This looks like a joint commission. The definition says "States, tribes, local governments, companies, unions, nonprofits, experts, and the general public are OUTSIDE it." It does not explicitly list foreign governments or their nationals. However, "people outside of the government" usually implies non-federal US entities or the general public. Foreign nationals are definitely outside the US federal government. But the key is "consult or coordinate... before making a decision." The Board *makes* the decisions. The US members vote as directed by the Secretary. So the Secretary is making the decision through the Board. The Panamanian members are voting independently? The text doesn't say. But the US side is controlled by the Secretary. This is effectively intra-governmental coordination (Secretary directing his appointees) plus a diplomatic arrangement. The definition's "No" trap for "consultation or coordination BETWEEN federal agencies or federal officials" is strong here for the US side. For the Panamanian side, it's a foreign government. The definition doesn't explicitly exclude foreign governments, but it focuses on "state or local governments, experts, the general public, companies, non-profit organizations". It doesn't mention foreign governments. However, the primary mechanism described is the Secretary directing the US members. This is internal control. The "participation" aspect is weak because the US government isn't consulting with outsiders; it's imposing its will through the Board. The Panamanian members are part of a treaty-based commission, not a typical advisory board of US outsiders. Given the strict "No" for intra-governmental coordination and the fact that the US members are effectively federal employees/officials acting under direct orders, this leans towards "No". The "outside" members are foreign nationals, which is a different category than the "outside" entities listed (states, tribes, public, etc.). The definition's examples of "Yes" are all domestic non-federal entities. I will label this "No" because the US decision-making is internal (Secretary directing votes) and the foreign members are part of a diplomatic commission, not a domestic public participation process.
